name: Cambridge diet

card.summary: The Cambridge diet is a very-low-calorie meal-replacement plan of shakes, soups and bars that people use to lose body fat quickly and look leaner.
card.note: The 1980s US version was linked to deaths; very-low-calorie diets are generally supervised medically.

quick.overview:
The Cambridge diet replaces normal meals with formula shakes, soups and bars, keeping daily calories very low so body weight and fat fall quickly. People use it to get leaner, whether for a visible change in face and body or ahead of an event.

It was developed in the 1960s by Alan Howard at Cambridge University for hospital weight-loss use and sold in the US from 1980. Randomized trials in clinics have studied it, mostly in obese patients, for weight loss and for keeping weight off afterwards.
quick.how: In the original form, formula products replaced all food for a period, then regular food was reintroduced in stages. The current UK version is organised in steps, beginning with a few products a day totalling a few hundred calories, and is classed as a very-low-calorie diet.
quick.risks: Reports in the early 1980s linked deaths to the US liquid diet; the FDA said eight deaths were potentially linked, and a UK working group in 1987 questioned how well it spared protein. NHS guidance says diets below 1,000 kcal a day should not exceed 12 weeks and below 600 kcal need medical supervision. Lean tissue loss is a documented concern.

lead: The Cambridge diet is a very-low-calorie diet (VLCD) built around meal-replacement formulas such as shakes, soups and bars. It was developed in the 1960s by Alan Howard at Cambridge University for hospital weight-loss programmes. [1]

People use very-low-calorie plans like it to lose body fat quickly, which reveals facial and body definition; the diet's appearance payoff is leanness. Clinic studies of Cambridge-type formula diets have followed obese patients through the initial loss and weight maintenance. [2][3]

The US product launched commercially in 1980 through multi-level marketing and was changed from 330 kcal a day to 800 kcal a day under FDA pressure after deaths in dieters. [1] The UK version was renamed the 1:1 Diet in 2019. [1]

chain: Formula meals replace food at very low calories
angle.text: The plan creates a large calorie deficit with nutritionally fortified formulas, so weight falls quickly. People use it to reach a leaner look, typically in short periods.

paras: The diet is mainly liquid, including soups, shakes, bars and meals. A 2006 figure for three servings of the liquid diet gave 43 g protein, 42 g carbohydrate and 8 g fat plus added micronutrients. [1] The current UK plan has six steps, the first requiring three to four products totalling at least 600 kcal a day. [1]

Cambridge Direct Sales obtained the US rights to the original powder in 1979 and launched in 1980. [1] In 1985 the company paid a settlement to the family of a 31-year-old woman who died while on the diet, and the FDA said eight deaths were potentially linked. [1] Journals of the time carried commentary on the formula and on deaths. [5][6][7]

In 1987 a UK government working group criticised the company's evidence and was not convinced the diet spared protein as well as conventional diets. [1] Cambridge Nutritional Foods has made the UK product since 2005. [1]

In a randomized trial, 60 obese patients began on a 330 kcal-a-day Cambridge diet for 12 weeks, then were randomized to balanced hypocaloric diets with or without the formula sachets during a maintenance period of 64 weeks. [3] A crossover trial in 17 obese women compared the Cambridge diet with a milk diet and measured nitrogen loss, with the Cambridge diet showing greater daily nitrogen loss at some points. [4]

Trials of very-low-calorie diets note that they reduce weight even in patients who failed conventional diets but that maintaining the loss is hard; randomized trials tested dexfenfluramine to aid maintenance after such diets. [8][9] Wikipedia summarises evidence as showing short-term weight loss but little long-term benefit. [1]

Besides the early deaths, a 1989 letter in The Lancet discussed sudden death and the diet. [7] Studies of very-low-calorie diets examine loss of fat, water and protein. [10] NHS guidance says diets under 1,000 kcal a day should not last beyond 12 weeks, and under 600 kcal require medical supervision; the American Academy of Family Physicians advised avoiding fad diets like this in 2005. [1]

Randomized trials have used the Cambridge diet as the very-low-calorie phase for obese patients, comparing weight maintenance strategies and a milk-based diet. [3][4] A trial of drug therapy after such diets and a trial of dexfenfluramine after initial weight control are also reported. [8][9] Studies used patients with obesity, not people seeking cosmetic leanness.
